abstract: Social bees, including bumble bees, host a community of microbes in their gut consisting of core bacterial taxa as well as non-core bacteria and fungi. Bumble bee research colonies from commercial suppliers are often utilized in research characterizing and examining the functions of bee microbiomes. However, commercial rearing conditions have the potential to shift the microbiome associated with bees, calling into question whether results obtained using commercial colonies are applicable to wild bees. Here, we examine differences between the microbiome of commercially-reared and wild caught bumble bees of three species (Bombus impatiens, B. terrestris, and B. vosnesenskii) using amplicon sequencing and qPCR to characterize bacterial and fungal communities within bee guts. We found that while all bee species hosted some microbes belonging to the core bumble bee gut community, microbial community composition and diversity varied between species and sources, with wild individuals lacking some groups of core bacteria and hosting a greater diversity of non-core bacterial and fungal taxa. This work highlights the presence and potential dominance of non-core microbial taxa within wild bumble bee gut communities, especially early in the colony life cycle. Overall, we conclude that rearing conditions can shape the composition of bumble bee microbiomes, and research on commercial colonies alone may overlook environmental taxa commonly associated with bees.
